title: Preprocessing & hypothesis tests
summary: Transform features using training statistics and use statistical tests whose assumptions match the data.
why: Prevents scale artifacts, leakage, and unsupported conclusions from noisy samples.
interview: Interpret a p-value, choose a test, and separate effect size from significance.
derivation: Pearson measures linear association; Spearman computes association of ranks and captures monotonic relationships. Neither identifies causality. Robust scaling uses a training median and an interquartile range.

A p-value is the probability, assuming the null model, of a statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not P(null is true). Type I error rejects a true null; Type II error misses a false null; power is 1-beta.

steps.note: Split by time or entity when random splitting leaks information.
Handle constant features and outliers explicitly.
steps.transformation: Estimate location and scale; persist parameters

steps.note: Student t: two means under its assumptions; Welch relaxes equal variance; ANOVA: omnibus mean comparison; chi-square: categorical independence.
Correct for multiple comparisons and state test assumptions.

traps: Fitting preprocessing before a split leaks evaluation data.
A significant ANOVA does not identify which pairs differ.
Sparse expected cell counts weaken chi-square approximation.
Failing to reject the null does not prove equivalence.
tradeoff: Robust methods tolerate outliers; power depends on sample size, variance, effect size, and the test design.
code:
from statistics import mean, stdev

def fit_standardizer(train):
    mu, sigma = mean(train), stdev(train)
    return lambda x: (x-mu)/(sigma or 1.0)

transform = fit_standardizer([1.,2.,3.])
assert transform(2.) == 0.0
assert transform(4.) == 2.0

explanations.title: Choose transformations using the training split
paragraphs: Standardization subtracts a training mean and divides by a training standard deviation. Min-max scaling uses training extrema. Robust scaling uses a training median and interquartile range. None should be refit on validation, test, or future production batches.

Outliers strongly affect mean, standard deviation, and range. A zero-variance column needs explicit handling. Tree split ordering often makes monotone feature scaling unnecessary, while distance methods, regularized linear models, and SVMs can change substantially with scale.

Pearson measures linear association. Spearman applies correlation to ranks and measures monotonic association. A monotonic curved relation can have strong Spearman association without being linear. Ties, outliers, missingness, and restricted ranges affect interpretation; correlation does not establish causality.

explanations.title: Null hypotheses, p-values, and power
paragraphs: Specify a null model, an alternative, an effect metric, and a decision rule before examining the result. A p-value is the probability under the null of a statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability that the null is true.

Type I error rejects a true null, controlled at alpha when assumptions and procedure hold. Type II error fails to reject a false null; its probability beta depends on effect size, sample size, noise, and test design. Power is 1-beta.

Report an effect estimate and uncertainty, not only significance. Large samples can make a negligible effect significant, while small samples may miss an important effect. Repeated peeking or testing many hypotheses requires an appropriate sequential or multiple-testing plan.

explanations.title: t-test, ANOVA, chi-square, and an experiment trace
paragraphs: Use an independent two-sample t procedure for two independent group means under suitable sampling assumptions. Welch handles unequal variances; a paired t-test instead operates on within-pair differences. These are different study designs.

One-way ANOVA tests whether all group means are equal across several independent groups. A significant result does not identify the differing pair; planned contrasts or corrected post-hoc comparisons answer that question. A chi-square independence test compares observed and expected counts in a contingency table and needs adequate expected counts.

For a latency experiment, randomize independent units, define the measurement window, compute an effect and confidence interval, and check distribution and independence assumptions. Repeated requests from the same user are correlated; treating every request as an independent unit can understate uncertainty.
